title: Halal food today
hook: certification, supply chains, and the spirit of tayyib

segments.voice: Yesterday, green mosques: panels on the roof, slow taps at the wudu station, the whole earth a masjid. Your line was mosques going green. Did you find one thing a place near you does? Today, from the roof to the plate. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-five.

A small logo in the corner of a package of chicken. A crescent, maybe, or a word in Arabic letters, and the name of an organization you've never heard of. Behind that little mark there's a whole chain: a farm, a slaughterhouse, a factory, a truck, a freezer, an inspector with a clipboard. A shopper glances at it for half a second and puts the package in the cart. Today, halal food, and the second word in the verse that stands behind the logo, the one that never fits on a label.
screen: `A SMALL LOGO.` → `A WHOLE CHAIN BEHIND IT.` → `THE WORD THAT DOESN'T FIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, from Surah al-Baqarah, in Pickthall: "O mankind! Eat of that which is lawful and wholesome in the earth." Notice who it's addressed to: mankind, everyone at the table. And notice there are two words, not one. Lawful is halal: what's permitted. The Qur'an names what isn't, in Surah al-Ma'idah: carrion, blood, pork, and meat dedicated to anything other than Allah. Wholesome is tayyib: good, pure, pleasant. Halal is a line. Tayyib is a quality. Now the modern part. A certifying body checks the halal side: how the animal was slaughtered, whether a gelatin came from pork, whether a flavoring hides alcohol, whether the halal meat touched other meat on the line. That's the supply chain, and it's real work. Certifiers and scholars don't all agree on the details, like whether an animal may be stunned before slaughter, or whether a machine may do the cutting. And some Muslims read another verse in al-Ma'idah, that the food of the People of the Book is lawful, as covering meat from Jews and Christians today, while others don't. Then the second word asks more than any stamp. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says that Allah has prescribed excellence in everything, and that when you slaughter, you should do it well: sharpen the blade, and spare the animal suffering. Some Muslims hear in that tayyib reaching back up the chain, to how the animal lived and died. Some Muslims now ask the same of the workers and the land. The logo can say halal. Only the whole chain can say good.
screen: `TWO WORDS: LAWFUL AND WHOLESOME.` · `HALAL IS A LINE. TAYYIB IS A QUALITY.` · `THE CERTIFIER CHECKS THE CHAIN.` · `SHARPEN THE BLADE, SPARE THE ANIMAL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one label, starting with the last thing you ate. Settle, and breathe. Bring it to mind: the bowl, the wrapper, the plate. Now trace it backward, one link at a time. Who sold it. Who carried it. Who made it. Where it grew, or how it lived. You won't know most of the answers, and that's the point: notice how long the chain is. If you pray, you can hold the two words together, lawful and wholesome, and offer thanks the way you usually do. If you don't, simply thank one link in the chain. The bell holds the time.
Halal food today. Food checked as lawful, from a certifier's stamp all the way back to the farm, with tayyib, wholesome and good, asking for more. Today's word.

Your line: lawful and good. Today, read one food label all the way through, and ask one question about the chain behind it. Tomorrow, Islamic finance today. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Muslims who keep halal often look for certification marks on meat and packaged food, check ingredient lists for things like pork gelatin or alcohol, and differ among themselves on questions such as stunning and the meat of the People of the Book.

fork.setup: you're a butcher, and you've got an animal to slaughter. according to the hadith in Sahih Muslim, what's asked of you?
options: just say the right words; the rest doesn't matter.
do it well: sharpen the blade, spare the animal suffering.
do it quickly, however it's done.
fork.reveal: the hadith says Allah has prescribed excellence in everything: sharpen the blade, and spare the animal. the law and the kindness come in one breath.

original.note: Arabic: good, wholesome, pure; the word paired with halal in 2:168.

trapdoor: what you thought: halal is a logo on a package.
what it means: halal is the lawful line; tayyib, wholesome and good, asks how the food was raised, slaughtered and handled.
what a scholar hears: halal and tayyib paired in 2:168; the forbidden list in 5:3; the food of the People of the Book in 5:5; the hadith of excellence in slaughter in Sahih Muslim.

sources.quoted: O mankind! Eat of that which is lawful and wholesome in the earth

sources.ref: Qur'an 5:3 (carrion, blood, swine-flesh, what is dedicated to other than Allah)
Qur'an 5:5 (the food of the People of the Book)
Sahih Muslim 1955 (Shaddad ibn Aws: excellence in everything; sharpen the blade)

notes: Confirm Pickthall's wording for 2:168 exactly as quoted.
5:3's list is summarized and shortened (it also names strangled and beaten animals and others); confirm the summary.
Debates named: stunning before slaughter, machine slaughter, and whether 5:5 covers meat from Jews and Christians today. Confirm these are fairly described without ranking positions.
'Some Muslims now ask the same of the workers and the land' refers to ethical or 'tayyib' food movements; no specific group is named.
Editor: the Sahih Muslim hadith speaks of excellence (ihsan), not of tayyib, so linking it to tayyib is now framed as how some Muslims hear it rather than as the narrator's statement.
